clues.title: Google car: Red car meta
text: A red Google car, with or without an antenna, in Generation 3 and on crappy roads is always Ukraine. However, the car may not always be visible, so don’t rule out Ukraine if you don’t see it.

clues.title: Skinny Ukraine
text: **3 Zebra Stripes**: Estonia, Lithuania, Russia, Ukraine. > Cross off Estonia and Russia (detailed guy in Estonia, Yellow borders in Russia) and you're left with Lithuania and Ukraine. Lithuania's guy is a liiittle bit more **fat** in the torso than Ukraine and the blue is generally more vibrant than Ukraine.

clues.title: Bad Road Quality
text: On average, Ukraine has some of the worst roads in Europe.
Most rural roads have lots of potholes, cracks and warped pavement.
This abysmal road quality can really help with tough 50-50s with Russia, which generally has somewhat better roads.

clues.title: Coverage: Red Car
text: All coverage in Ukraine is Generation 3.
Most of it was made using a red Google car.
This car is almost unique to Ukraine.
It sometimes has an antenna, and sometimes no antenna.
You will not find the red Generation 3 car in Russia.

clues.title: Landscape: Mountains
text: The Carpathian Mountains is an area in western Ukraine that is significantly hillier than the rest of the country, in some places bordering on mountainous. It is also much more forested, with very little agriculture, and a lot of pine trees. The roads going through it tend to be more curvy, rather than the straight highways found in the rest of the country.

clues.title: Landscape: South Fields
text: Towards the south, the climate becomes warm and dry. The landscape is rather arid. Larger Forests are quite rare and make way for shrubs and open fields.

clues.title: Architecture: Single Family Homes
text: Single-family homes are very common in suburbs and small towns.
These neighbourhoods are often heavily vegetated and tend to look rundown.
Most roads are unpaved.
Buildings are usually made of bricks, often have corrugated roofs, and are invariably surrounded by fences.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Polish Bollards
text: These “Polish” bollards can be found in the Zakarpattia Oblast. They have a red reflector that wraps around the bollard.
They are identical to the standard bollard used in Poland (hence the name).

clues.title: Plate: Ukraine
text: Ukraine uses long, white licence plates, with a distinctive blue and yellow strip on the left (the colours of the flag).
You may also come across older plates, where the blue and yellow are difficult to spot.
NOTE: Russia uses fully white licence plates, without a strip on the left.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Donetsk coverage
text: Donetsk and Odesa are the only 2 cities that only have 2011 coverage, all the coverage within those cities is taken in the autumn, which means you will see many orange and yellow leaves on the trees. Donetsk has long antenna, Odesa has short antenna.
NOTE: Kyiv, Lviv and Kharkiv also have autumn coverage but the majority has been overwritten by the newer summer coverage so you will rarely see those cities in autumn aswell.

clues.title: Language: Ukrainian
text: Ukrainian is an East Slavic language related to Russian and Belarusian. Ukrainian uses the Cyrillic script. These letters are unique to Ukrainian, compared to Russian: **Ґ ґ**, **І і**, **Ї ї** and **Є є** (not to be confused with Э э in Russian and Belarusian).
The Ukrainian word for street is **вулиця** (vulytsya), abbreviated **вул.** (vul.). The Russian word is **улица** (ulitsa), abbreviated **ул.** (ul.), without a **в** (v) at the beginning.

The Ukrainian word for city is **місто** (misto), abbreviated **м.** (m.). It can be used both to differentiate it from Russian where the word for city is **город** (gorod), abbreviated **г.** (g.), and to quickly find the city name in addresses.
